topic.title: Competition, producers and food webs
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Usually the opening question of the B1 paper, built round one named habitat and worth eight to twelve marks in total: identify the habitat, name the energy source, complete a food web with arrows, identify trophic levels, explain a population change and do one percentage calculation. Most of it is well answered; the marks that move are the Sun, the word 'compete', the arrow direction and the denominator.
mustMemorise: The Sun is the source of energy for most ecosystems
Producers are green plants; they capture the Sun's energy by photosynthesis
Level 1 producer, Level 2 primary consumer, Level 3 secondary consumer, Level 4 tertiary consumer
An arrow runs FROM the organism eaten TO the organism that eats it
Arrows show consumption and the transfer of energy and of carbon and nitrogen
Plants compete for water, light, space, minerals
Animals compete for water, food, territory, mates, and must avoid predators
notOnThisSpec: Pyramids of number, biomass or energy
Percentage efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels
Predator-prey cycle graphs as a named topic
Named adaptations of particular species (learn the idea, not a list)

note.title: Competition, producers and food webs
note.subject: science

mustKnow: The Sun is the energy source; green plants are the producers
Level 1 producer → Level 2 primary → Level 3 secondary → Level 4 tertiary consumer
An arrow means 'is eaten by' and shows energy and substances moving
Plants compete for water, light, space, minerals
Animals compete for water, food, territory, mates, and avoid predators

notOnThisSpec: Pyramids of number, biomass or energy
Predator-prey cycles as a named topic
Interspecific and intraspecific competition as terms

mustBeAbleTo: Name the Sun as the source of energy for an ecosystem
Explain why green plants are called producers
Identify producers and consumers from a food web
Give the trophic level of any organism in a web, one level at a time
Say what an arrow represents, and draw it the right way round
Give the four resources plants compete for and the four animals compete for
Explain a decline as competition rather than predation
Follow a change through a web from one organism to the next
Calculate a percentage increase or decrease, dividing by the original value
Explain how removing a habitat reduces biodiversity
sheet.howExamined: B1 Foundation (60 marks, 1 hour) and B1 Higher (70 marks, 1 hour), calculator allowed; these outcomes are common to both tiers. It is normally the opening question, worth eight to twelve marks across several short parts hung on one habitat, with a food web to complete and one percentage calculation. Schemes are point-for-point and short: [1] per organism, [1] per arrow, [1] per resource.
traps: Naming a part of a plant as the source of energy instead of the Sun (March 2026 B1 F Q6)
Describing a competitor as a predator (March 2026 B1 F Q6)
Giving an animal for trophic Level 1 (March 2026 B1 F Q6)
Drawing food-web arrows pointing at the food instead of the feeder
Placing the organisms in a web but not adding the arrows (Summer 2025 B1 H Q1)
Dividing a percentage change by the final value (Summer 2025 B1 H Q1)
Writing an explanation that stops one link short of the quantity asked about

steps.working: The ladybird eats the aphid, so removing ladybirds removes one of the aphid's predators.
steps.decision: Start by naming the feeding relationship from the web. An explanation that never mentions who eats whom is not using the web.

steps.working: Fewer aphids are eaten, so the number of aphids increases.
steps.decision: Say which way the number moves, and why. 'The aphids change' earns nothing.

steps.working: Aphids feed on the wheat, so more aphids means more wheat is eaten.
steps.decision: Follow the arrow down a level. The web tells you the aphid's food without you having to know anything about aphids.
Finish with the answer to the question actually asked. A chain of reasoning that stops one step short of the yield loses the last mark.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Ladybirds eat aphids, so removing the ladybirds removes one of the aphid's predators and fewer aphids are eaten. The number of aphids therefore increases. Aphids feed on the wheat, so more aphids means more wheat is eaten and the wheat yield falls.

twin.stem: Foxes were removed from the area around the hedgerow. Use the food web to explain what would happen to the number of rabbits and then to the hawthorn.

accepted: the fox eats the rabbit, so with the foxes gone fewer rabbits are eaten and the number of rabbits increases, and because rabbits feed on the hawthorn more of it is eaten, so there is less hawthorn left

items.stem: What is the source of energy for almost every ecosystem on Earth?
items.skill: Name the Sun as the energy source

options.feedback: The Sun. Green plants capture its light energy by photosynthesis and make it available to everything else.
The leaves capture the energy; they are not its source. March 2026 examiners reported parts of a tree given instead of the Sun.
The soil supplies water and minerals, not energy.
Producers are how the energy enters the web, but the energy itself comes from the Sun.

items.stem: An arrow in a food chain points from a grass plant to a rabbit. What does it show?
items.skill: Read the direction of an arrow

options.text: energy and substances passing from the grass into the rabbit
options.feedback: The arrow shows consumption and the transfer of energy and substances. Read it as 'is eaten by'.

options.text: the rabbit being eaten by the grass, because the arrow points at what is eaten
options.feedback: The arrow points at the eater, not at the food. Drawn the other way round it would say the grass eats the rabbit.

options.text: the grass and the rabbit competing for space
options.feedback: Food-web arrows never show competition; they show feeding.

options.text: the rabbit returning nutrients to the grass
options.feedback: That happens through decomposition, and it is not what a food-chain arrow shows.

items.stem: Which of these do plants NOT compete for?
items.skill: Separate the plant and animal resource lists

options.feedback: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis, so they never compete for it. They compete for water, light, space and minerals.
Light is one of the four: a tall plant shading a short one is competition for light.
Minerals are one of the four. Roots growing through the same soil compete for nitrate.
Space is one of the four: room for roots below and leaves above.

items.stem: Grey squirrels were introduced to a wood and the red squirrel population fell. Which sentence would score?

options.text: The greys competed with the reds for food and nesting sites, so the reds had less of both.
options.feedback: Competition for a named resource. That is the relationship the mark scheme rewards.

options.text: The greys hunted and ate the red squirrels.
options.feedback: Greys do not eat reds. March 2026 examiners reported exactly this answer, and it earns nothing.

options.text: The reds were at a lower trophic level than the greys.
options.feedback: Both squirrels eat the same food, so they are at the same trophic level. The issue is competition, not levels.

options.text: The greys are better adapted, so the reds died out naturally.
options.feedback: Close, but it never names what they are better at. Say what resource is being competed for.

context.setting: A wheat field beside a hawthorn hedge

figures.alt: A food web of nine organisms in four rows, joined by eleven arrows: wheat to aphid, wheat to wood mouse, hawthorn to aphid, hawthorn to rabbit, aphid to ladybird, aphid to blue tit, ladybird to blue tit, wood mouse to kestrel, wood mouse to fox, rabbit to fox, and blue tit to kestrel.

parts.stem:
Use the food web.
Name the two producers.

scheme.for: wheat and hawthorn (both needed)

hints: Producers are the green plants.

commonErrors.feedback: Those are all consumers. A producer is a green plant that makes its own food by photosynthesis.

parts.stem: Name one primary consumer in the web.

scheme.for: aphid / wood mouse / rabbit

hints: A primary consumer eats a producer.
parts.workedSolution: The aphid (or the wood mouse, or the rabbit).

parts.stem: State what the arrow between the aphid and the ladybird shows.

accepted: the aphid is eaten by the ladybird, so energy and substances pass from the aphid to the ladybird

scheme.for: the aphid is eaten by the ladybird / the direction energy and substances are transferred

hints: Read the arrow as 'is eaten by'.
parts.workedSolution: That the aphid is eaten by the ladybird, so energy and substances such as carbon and nitrogen are transferred from the aphid to the ladybird.

pattern.regex: aphid eats the ladybird|ladybird is eaten by the aphid

commonErrors.feedback: The arrow points at the eater. Here it points at the ladybird, so the ladybird eats the aphid.

context.setting: The same web, with the trophic levels asked one at a time

figures.alt: A food web of nine organisms in four rows, joined by eleven arrows: wheat to aphid, wheat to wood mouse, hawthorn to aphid, hawthorn to rabbit, aphid to ladybird, aphid to blue tit, ladybird to blue tit, wood mouse to kestrel, wood mouse to fox, rabbit to fox, and blue tit to kestrel.

parts.stem: Which organism in the web is at trophic Level 1?

options.feedback: Level 1 is always the producers, and wheat is a green plant.
The aphid eats the wheat, so it is at Level 2.
The blue tit eats aphids and ladybirds, so it is at Level 3 or 4.
The fox is a top predator. March 2026 examiners reported foxes offered for Level 1.

scheme.for: wheat

hints: Level 1 can only be a plant.

parts.stem: Which organism is a primary consumer, at trophic Level 2?

options.feedback: Hawthorn is a plant, so it is a producer at Level 1.
The rabbit eats hawthorn, a producer, so it is a primary consumer.
The ladybird eats aphids, which are primary consumers, so it is at Level 3.
The kestrel eats wood mice and blue tits, so it is at the top of its chains.

scheme.for: rabbit

hints: A primary consumer eats a producer.

parts.stem: Which organism eats a secondary consumer, and so can be a tertiary consumer?

options.feedback: The aphid eats plants, so it is a primary consumer.
The wood mouse eats wheat, so it is a primary consumer.
The blue tit eats the ladybird, which is a secondary consumer, so in that chain the blue tit is a tertiary consumer.
Hawthorn is a producer. It eats nothing.

scheme.for: blue tit
accept: kestrel, via wheat → aphid → blue tit → kestrel

hints: Find something with an arrow coming into it from the ladybird.
parts.workedSolution: The blue tit, because it eats the ladybird, which is itself a secondary consumer.

context.setting: Two bird species nesting in the same small wood

parts.stem: Give two resources that plants compete for.

scheme.for: any two from: water / light / space / minerals — [1] each

hints: Four are named in the specification, and food is not one of them.
parts.workedSolution: Water and light are two of them: every plant in the bed needs both, and there is not enough of either to go round. (Space and minerals would do just as well.)

commonErrors.feedback: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis, so they never compete for it. The four are water, light, space and minerals.

parts.stem:
A new bird species arrives in a wood and starts nesting in the same holes as an existing species. The existing species declines.
Explain why, without using the word 'eats'.

accepted: the two species compete for the same nest holes, and because there is a limited number of them fewer of the original species can breed successfully

scheme.for: the two species compete for the same resource
the nest sites are limited, so fewer of the original species can breed and its numbers fall
reject: the new bird eats the old one
scheme.examinerNote: March 2026: some candidates described a competitor as a predator.

hints: Name the relationship, then say what runs out.
parts.workedSolution: The two species compete for the same nest holes. There is only a limited number of holes, so if the new species takes some of them fewer of the original species can breed, and its population falls.

commonErrors.feedback: Two species using the same resource are competitors, not predator and prey. Say what they are competing for.

context.setting: A woodland clearing in early summer

parts.stem: Name the source of energy for a woodland ecosystem.

scheme.for: the Sun
scheme.examinerNote: March 2026 B1 F Q6(a)(ii): quite a few candidates gave part of the tree as the energy source instead of the Sun.

hints: Where does the energy enter the whole system from?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the part of the plant that captures the energy, not the source of it. The energy comes from the Sun.

parts.stem: Explain why green plants are called producers.

accepted: they capture light energy from the Sun and use it in photosynthesis to produce their own food, which makes that energy available to every consumer in the ecosystem

scheme.for: they capture light energy from the Sun and produce their own food by photosynthesis
so they make that energy available to the consumers that eat them

hints: Produce what, from what?
parts.workedSolution: Green plants capture light energy from the Sun and use it in photosynthesis to produce their own food, glucose. Because everything else in the ecosystem feeds on plants directly or indirectly, the producers make the Sun's energy available to the whole web.

context.setting: A farmer sprays a pesticide that kills ladybirds as well as pest insects

figures.alt: A food web of nine organisms in four rows, joined by eleven arrows: wheat to aphid, wheat to wood mouse, hawthorn to aphid, hawthorn to rabbit, aphid to ladybird, aphid to blue tit, ladybird to blue tit, wood mouse to kestrel, wood mouse to fox, rabbit to fox, and blue tit to kestrel.

parts.stem:
Before the spray there were 120 aphids per square metre of wheat. Six weeks after it, there were 486.
Calculate the percentage increase in the number of aphids.
Show your working out.

scheme.for: increase = 486 − 120 = 366
divides by the ORIGINAL number: 366 ÷ 120 × 100

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 B1 H Q1(d) and March 2026 B1 H Q7(b): some candidates used the wrong denominator, and others showed no working.

hints: Percentage increase = increase ÷ starting value × 100.
Show the subtraction on its own line: it carries a mark by itself.

commonErrors.feedback: Divided by the final number instead of the starting number. The denominator is always the value you started from, here 120.

parts.stem: Use the food web to explain the rise in aphid numbers after the spray.

accepted: the spray killed the ladybirds, which eat aphids, so one of the aphid's predators was removed, fewer aphids were eaten and the aphid population rose

scheme.for: the spray killed the ladybirds
ladybirds eat aphids, so one of the aphid's predators was removed
fewer aphids were eaten, so more survived and bred and the population rose

hints: Start with what the spray did.
Then follow the arrow into the ladybird and out of it.
parts.workedSolution: The spray killed the ladybirds. Ladybirds eat aphids, so one of the aphid's predators was removed from the web. With fewer ladybirds eating them, more aphids survived and bred, so the aphid population rose.

commonErrors.feedback: The arrow runs from the aphid to the ladybird, which means the ladybird eats the aphid.

parts.stem:
The wheat yield fell from 8.4 tonnes per hectare to 6.3 tonnes per hectare.
Calculate the percentage decrease in yield.
hints: Same rule as part (a), with a decrease instead of an increase.
parts.workedSolution: Decrease = 8.4 − 6.3 = 2.1 tonnes per hectare. Percentage decrease = 2.1 ÷ 8.4 × 100 = 25%.

commonErrors.feedback: Divided by the new yield instead of the old one. 2.1 ÷ 6.3 × 100 gives 33.3%; the starting value goes on the bottom.

context.setting: Four organisms from the web, to be put into one chain

figures.alt: One food chain of four boxes joined by three arrows: wheat, aphid, ladybird, blue tit.

parts.stem:
Put these four organisms into a food chain, starting with the producer.

ladybird · wheat · blue tit · aphid

scheme.for: wheat first, as the producer
aphid second, as the primary consumer
ladybird then blue tit
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 B1 H Q1(a): most candidates placed the organisms but fewer added the lines and arrows linking them.

hints: Start with the green plant.
Then follow who eats whom up the chain.
parts.workedSolution: wheat → aphid → ladybird → blue tit. The arrows point from each organism to the one that eats it.

commonErrors.feedback: The chain has been written from the top predator down. A food chain starts with the producer, because that is where the energy enters.

context.setting: A hedge removed to make one large field

figures.alt: A food web of nine organisms in four rows, joined by eleven arrows: wheat to aphid, wheat to wood mouse, hawthorn to aphid, hawthorn to rabbit, aphid to ladybird, aphid to blue tit, ladybird to blue tit, wood mouse to kestrel, wood mouse to fox, rabbit to fox, and blue tit to kestrel.

parts.stem:
A farmer removes the hawthorn hedge to make one larger field.
Suggest two effects this would have on the organisms in the food web.

accepted: the rabbits lose their food supply so their numbers fall, and the foxes then have less to eat so their numbers fall too

scheme.for: any two from: rabbits lose a food source so their numbers fall / foxes have less prey so their numbers fall / aphids lose one of their two food plants / nesting and shelter sites for blue tits are lost / biodiversity of the field falls — [1] each

hints: Follow the arrows out of the hawthorn.
Then follow the arrows out of whatever fed on it.
parts.workedSolution: The rabbits lose one of their food sources, so their numbers fall; the foxes then have less prey and their numbers fall too. (The aphids also lose one of their two food plants, and blue tits lose nesting and shelter sites.)

parts.stem: Explain why removing the hedge reduces the biodiversity of the farm.

accepted: the hedge is a habitat that supplies food and shelter for species that cannot live in the open field, so when it goes those species disappear and the number of different species on the farm falls

scheme.for: the hedge is a habitat providing food, shelter and nest sites that the open field does not
so the species that depend on it are lost and the number of different species present falls

hints: Biodiversity counts species, not individuals.
parts.workedSolution: The hedge is a habitat in its own right, supplying food, shelter and nest sites that an open wheat field does not. Removing it removes the only place those species can live, so they disappear from the farm and the number of different species present — the biodiversity — falls.

findTheMistake.stem:
Sean is asked: 'Red squirrels have become rare in a wood since grey squirrels arrived. Explain why, and name the source of energy for the wood. [3]'
His answer:
studentWorking: The grey squirrels hunt the red squirrels and eat them.
That is why there are fewer reds now.
The source of energy for the wood is the Sun.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Grey squirrels do not eat red squirrels. The two species **compete** for the same food and the same nest sites, and the greys are larger and can eat a wider range of food, so the reds are left with less.
correction: The grey squirrels compete with the red squirrels for food and for nest sites.
The greys can eat a wider range of food, so the reds get less and fewer survive and breed.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark from three: the source of energy is right. The two marks you missed are not hard. Before writing 'eats', check whether the two organisms actually appear in the same food chain — if they eat the same things, the word you want is **compete**. And keep the energy habit: in an ecosystem question the source is almost always the **Sun**; the plant is what captures it.

prompts.prompt: What is the source of energy for most ecosystems, and what captures it?
prompts.answer: The Sun. Green plants — the producers — capture it by photosynthesis and make it available to consumers.

prompts.prompt: What does an arrow in a food chain represent?
prompts.answer: Consumption, and the transfer of energy and substances such as carbon and nitrogen. It runs from the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it.

prompts.prompt: What do plants compete for, and what do animals compete for?
prompts.answer: Plants: water, light, space, minerals. Animals: water, food, territory, mates, and they must avoid predators. Plants never compete for food.

prompts.prompt: Two species decline when a third arrives, but none of them eats the others. What is the relationship called?
prompts.answer: Competition — they need the same limited resource. Calling a competitor a predator is the error examiners report on the squirrel question.

prompts.prompt: Which trophic level holds the producers, and what can never be at that level?
prompts.answer: Level 1 holds the producers, which are green plants. No animal can be at Level 1.
